=∑i=1dxi2​xi2+∑i=1d∑j=1,j≠idxi2​xj2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{2}x_{i}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{d}x_{i}^{2}x_{j}^{2}
=∑i=1dxi4+∑i=1d∑j=1,j≠idxi2​xj2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{4}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{d}x_{i}^{2}x_{j}^{2}
≥∑i=1dxi4=∥𝐱⊙2∥22,\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{4}=\lVert{{\mathbf{x}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}^{2},

as the omitted term is the sum of non-negative numbers. ∎

Proposition 7.

Let m≥2m\geq 2 be an integer. Let 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱m∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where

𝐱i=(xi​j)j∈[d]\mathbf{x}_{i}=\left(x_{ij}\right)_{j\in[d]}

for i∈[m]i\in[m]. For i∈[m]i\in[m], let 𝐱i⊙2{\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\odot 2}} denote the entry-wise square of 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i}. Then

∥𝐱1⊙𝐱2⊙⋯⊙𝐱m∥2≤∥𝐱1⊙2∥2∥𝐱2⊙2∥2⋯∥𝐱m⊙2∥2\lVert{\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}\odot\cdots\odot\mathbf{x}_{m}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\cdots\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{m}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}
Proof.

We prove this by induction. Consider the base case with m=2m=2. Then note that

∥𝐱1⊙𝐱2∥22=∑j=1dx1​j2​x2​j2=⟨𝐱1⊙2,𝐱2⊙2⟩\lVert{\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_{1j}^{2}x_{2j}^{2}=\langle{{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\odot 2}}},{{\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\odot 2}}}\rangle

Furthermore, ⟨𝐱1⊙2,𝐱2⊙2⟩≥0\langle{{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\odot 2}}},{{\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\odot 2}}}\rangle\geq 0, as it is the dot product of two vectors all elements of which are non-negative. Thus from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we get

⟨𝐱1⊙2,𝐱2⊙2⟩≤∥𝐱1⊙2∥2⋅∥𝐱2⊙2∥2\langle{{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\odot 2}}},{{\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\odot 2}}}\rangle\leq\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}

This immediately gives us

∥𝐱1⊙𝐱2∥2≤∥𝐱1⊙2∥2​∥𝐱2⊙2∥2\lVert{\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}

which proves the base case. Next assume that the statement is true for m=km=k, and consider

∥𝐱1⊙𝐱2⊙⋯⊙𝐱k+1∥2\lVert{\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}\odot\cdots\odot\mathbf{x}_{k+1}}\rVert_{2}

Now 𝐱1⊙𝐱2⊙⋯⊙𝐱k\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}\odot\cdots\odot\mathbf{x}_{k} is a vector in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Denote this by 𝐲\mathbf{y}. Then through the base case

∥𝐱1⊙𝐱2⊙⋯⊙𝐱k+1∥2=∥𝐲⊙𝐱k+1∥2≤∥𝐲⊙2∥2⋅∥𝐱k+1⊙2∥2\lVert{\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}\odot\cdots\odot\mathbf{x}_{k+1}}\rVert_{2}=\lVert{\mathbf{y}\odot\mathbf{x}_{k+1}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{y}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{k+1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}

From Proposition 6, we have

∥𝐲⊙2∥2≤∥𝐲∥22=∥𝐲∥2\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{y}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\leq\sqrt{\lVert{\mathbf{y}}\rVert_{2}^{2}}=\lVert{\mathbf{y}}\rVert_{2}

Thus,

∥𝐱1⊙𝐱2⊙⋯⊙𝐱k+1∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}\odot\cdots\odot\mathbf{x}_{k+1}}\rVert_{2} ≤∥𝐲∥2⋅∥𝐱k+1⊙2∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{\mathbf{y}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{k+1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}
=∥𝐱1⊙𝐱2⊙⋯⊙𝐱k∥2⋅∥𝐱k+1⊙2∥2\displaystyle=\lVert{\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}\odot\cdots\odot\mathbf{x}_{k}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{k+1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}
≤∥𝐱1⊙2∥2∥𝐱2⊙2∥2⋯∥𝐱k⊙2∥2∥𝐱k+1⊙2∥2\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\cdots\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{k}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}_{k+1}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}

which follows from the induction hypothesis. This proves the result. ∎

Proposition 8.

Let 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let 𝐲^\widehat{\mathbf{y}} be the normalized version of 𝐲\mathbf{y}. Then

∥𝐱⊙𝐲^∥2≤d⋅∥𝐱∥4\lVert{{\mathbf{x}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\rVert_{4}
Proof.

From Proposition 7, we have

∥𝐱⊙𝐲^∥2≤∥𝐱⊙2∥2⋅‖𝐲^⊙2‖2\lVert{{\mathbf{x}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\lVert{{\mathbf{x}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\left\lVert{{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\odot 2}}}\right\rVert_{2}}

where 𝐱⊙2{\mathbf{x}^{\odot 2}} and 𝐲^⊙2{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\odot 2}} are the entry-wise squares of 𝐱\mathbf{x} and y^\widehat{y}, respectively. From Proposition 6 we have

‖𝐲^⊙2‖2≤‖𝐲^‖22\left\lVert{{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\odot 2}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

And from Proposition 5 we have

‖𝐲^‖22≤d\left\lVert{\widehat{{\mathbf{y}}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq d

Thus,

‖𝐲^⊙2‖2≤d\sqrt{\left\lVert{{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\odot 2}}}\right\rVert_{2}}\leq\sqrt{d}

Finally, note that

(∥𝐱⊙2∥2)1/2\displaystyle({\lVert{{\mathbf{x}^{\odot 2}}}\rVert_{2}})^{1/2} =(((x12)2+(x22)2+⋯+(xd2)2)1/2)1/2\displaystyle=\left(\left((x_{1}^{2})^{2}+(x_{2}^{2})^{2}+\cdots+(x_{d}^{2})^{2}\right)^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}
=(x14+x24+⋯+xd4)1/4\displaystyle=\left(x_{1}^{4}+x_{2}^{4}+\cdots+x_{d}^{4}\right)^{1/4}
=∥𝐱∥4\displaystyle=\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\rVert_{4}

Combining these we get

∥𝐱⊙𝐲^∥2≤d⋅∥𝐱∥4\lVert{{\mathbf{x}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\rVert_{4} (4)

∎

5.3 Global Sensitivity Analysis

We now analyze global sensitivity (Definition 4) of the functions preceding the offloaded components. In our analysis, we use the same dimension dd for all operations. As discussed in Section 3.2, some components use different dimensions, e.g., dkeyd_{\text{key}}. However, this is merely an implementation issue, and our sensitivity analysis can be used by replacing dd with the exact dimension applicable to the operation.

5.3.1 Initial Tokens

As a warm-up we look at the initial layer, even though it is not offloaded. At initialization, the input prompt is converted into tokens, and then each token is represented by a token embedding 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The token embeddings are from the vocabulary 𝗏𝗈𝖼𝖺𝖻⊆ℝd\mathsf{vocab}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} of the LLM. Global sensitivity, in this case for an identity function, can be found experimentally as

max𝐱,𝐲∈𝗏𝗈𝖼𝖺𝖻⁡∥𝐱−𝐲∥2\max_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathsf{vocab}}\lVert{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}}\rVert_{2}

Note that we do not need to span the entire space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, since the token embeddings are only from 𝗏𝗈𝖼𝖺𝖻\mathsf{vocab}.

5.3.2 After Layer Normalization

The layer normalization function 𝖫𝖭:ℝd→ℝd\mathsf{LN}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} as defined in [5] is

𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱,𝜶,𝜷,γ)=𝜶⊙𝐱^+𝜷\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x};\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta},\gamma)={\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}+\bm{\beta} (5)

where 𝜶,𝜷∈ℝd\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are learned parameters, and 𝐱^\widehat{\mathbf{x}} is the z-score normalization of 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.1717 17 The parameter γ\gamma in the z-score normalization as defined in Definition 5 does not appear in [5] but it is used in actual implementations for numerical stability to ensure the denominator never becomes 0. In some models such as the new Llama models, 𝐱^\widehat{\mathbf{x}} is RMS normalized, known as the RMSNorm [40]. The benefit and use of the RMSNorm in Llama models is discussed in [17]. The following result holds for both standardization methods. We will mostly skip any reference to the parameters 𝜶,𝜷\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta} and γ\gamma, and simply write 𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x}) instead of 𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱,𝜶,𝜷,γ)\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x};\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta},\gamma) to avoid notational clutter.

Theorem 1.

Let 𝖫𝖭\mathsf{LN} be as defined in Eq. (5). Then its global sensitivity Δ​𝖫𝖭\Delta\mathsf{LN} satisfies

Δ​𝖫𝖭≤2​d⋅∥𝜶∥4\Delta\mathsf{LN}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}
Proof.

For any 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)−𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐲)∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})-\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})}\rVert_{2} =∥𝜶⊙𝐱^+𝜷−𝜶⊙𝐲^−𝜷∥2\displaystyle=\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}+\bm{\beta}-{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}-\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}
=∥𝜶⊙(𝐱^−𝐲^)∥2\displaystyle=\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}-\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}}\rVert_{2}
=∥𝜶⊙𝐱^−𝜶⊙𝐲^)∥2\displaystyle=\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}-{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}})}}\rVert_{2}
≤∥𝜶⊙𝐱^∥2+∥𝜶⊙𝐲^∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}}\rVert_{2}+\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}}\rVert_{2}

where in the last step we have used the triangle inequality for the Euclidean norm. From Proposition 8 we get

∥𝜶⊙𝐱^∥2≤d⋅∥𝜶∥4 and ∥𝜶⊙𝐲^∥2≤d⋅∥𝜶∥4\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}\quad\text{ and }\quad\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}

Putting these inequalities in the above inequality, we get

∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)−𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐲)∥2≤∥𝜶⊙𝐱^∥2+∥𝜶⊙𝐲^∥2≤2​d⋅∥𝜶∥4\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})-\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})}\rVert_{2}\leq\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}}\rVert_{2}+\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}}}\rVert_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}

Since 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} were arbitrary, we conclude

Δ​𝖫𝖭≤2​d⋅∥𝜶∥4\Delta\mathsf{LN}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}

∎

5.3.3 After the Attention Mechanism

The attention mechanism can be defined as follows. Let WqryW_{\text{qry}}, WkeyW_{\text{key}} and WvalW_{\text{val}} be d×dd\times d matrices. Suppose we have nn vectors 𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱n∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, define

𝐪i=Wqry⋅𝐱i,𝐤i=Wkey⋅𝐱i,𝐯i=Wval⋅𝐱i\mathbf{q}_{i}=W_{\text{qry}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i},\quad\mathbf{k}_{i}=W_{\text{key}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i},\quad\mathbf{v}_{i}=W_{\text{val}}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}

which are again vectors from ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let 𝐪=Wqry​𝐱\mathbf{q}=W_{\text{qry}}\mathbf{x} for some 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n define

pi​(𝐱)=exp⁡(⟨𝐪,𝐤i⟩/d)∑j=1nexp⁡(⟨𝐪,𝐤j⟩/d)=softmax​(⟨𝐪,𝐤i⟩d)p_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp(\langle{\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{k}_{i}}\rangle/\sqrt{d})}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(\langle{\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{k}_{j}}\rangle/\sqrt{d})}=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{\langle{\mathbf{q}},{\mathbf{k}_{i}}\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\right)

Note that ∑i=1npi​(𝐱)=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\mathbf{x})=1. With this, the attention mechanism for any 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is defined as

𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐱)=∑i=1npi​(𝐱)​𝐯i\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{v}_{i} (6)

The input to the attention function is in fact layer normalized. Thus, we can write it as

𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐱)\displaystyle\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{x}) =∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱i)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x}_{i})
=∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i+𝜷)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}+\bm{\beta}})
=∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)+∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅𝜷\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i})}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot\bm{\beta}
=∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)+(∑i=1npi​(𝐱^))​Wval⋅𝜷\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i})}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})\right)W_{\text{val}}\cdot\bm{\beta}
=Wval⋅𝜷+∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)\displaystyle=W_{\text{val}}\cdot\bm{\beta}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i})} (7)

where 𝐱^\widehat{\mathbf{x}} and 𝐱^i\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i} are normalized versions of 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} respectively. We are interested in finding Δ​𝖺𝗍𝗍\Delta\mathsf{att}.

Theorem 2.

Let 𝖺𝗍𝗍\mathsf{att} be as defined in Eq. (7). Then its global sensitivity Δ​𝖺𝗍𝗍\Delta\mathsf{att} satisfies

Δ​𝖺𝗍𝗍≤2​d⋅∥Wval∥2⋅∥𝜶∥4\Delta\mathsf{att}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}
Proof.

By definition, for any 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}

𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐱)=Wval⋅𝜷+∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{x})=W_{\text{val}}\cdot\bm{\beta}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}})

and

𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐲)=Wval⋅𝜷+∑i=1npi′​(𝐲^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i′)\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{y})=W_{\text{val}}\cdot\bm{\beta}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}p^{\prime}_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}})

Note that we use different variables pi′p^{\prime}_{i} and 𝐱^i′\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{i} for 𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐲)\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{y}) since replacing 𝐱\mathbf{x} with 𝐲\mathbf{y} changes the softmax probabilities pi​(𝐱^)p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}) and the sequence of vectors 𝐱^i\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i} due to one vector being different. Now

∥𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐱)−𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐲)∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{x})-\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{y})}\rVert_{2} =‖∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)−∑i=1npi′​(𝐲^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i′)‖2\displaystyle=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}})-\sum_{i=1}^{n}p^{\prime}_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2}
≤‖∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)‖2+‖∑i=1npi′​(𝐲^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i′)‖2\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{n}p^{\prime}_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2}
≤∑i=1n‖pi​(𝐱^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)‖2+∑i=1n‖pi′​(𝐲^)​Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i′)‖2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lVert p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lVert p^{\prime}_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2}
=∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​‖Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)‖2+∑i=1npi′​(𝐲^)​‖Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i′)‖2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})\left\lVert W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}p^{\prime}_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})\left\lVert W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2} (8)

where we have used standard properties of the Euclidean norm. Now let us examine first of the two norms above in isolation. Let 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n be fixed. From Eq. (3), We have

‖Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i)‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2} ≤∥Wval∥2⋅∥𝜶⊙𝐱^i∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{{\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\rVert_{2}
≤∥Wval∥2⋅d⋅∥𝜶∥4\displaystyle\leq\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}

where the second inequality follows from Proposition 5. Likewise, for any i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, we have

‖Wval⋅(𝜶⊙𝐱^i′)‖2≤∥Wval∥2⋅d⋅∥𝜶∥4\left\lVert W_{\text{val}}\cdot({\bm{\alpha}}\odot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}

Thus, Eq. (8) becomes

∥𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐱)−𝖺𝗍𝗍⁡(𝐲)∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{x})-\mathsf{att}(\mathbf{y})}\rVert_{2} ≤∑i=1npi​(𝐱^)​∥Wval∥2⋅d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∑i=1npi′​(𝐲^)​∥Wval∥2⋅d⋅∥𝜶∥4\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}p^{\prime}_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}
=(∑i=1npi​(𝐱^))​∥Wval∥2⋅d⋅∥𝜶∥4+(∑i=1npi′​(𝐲^))​∥Wval∥2⋅d⋅∥𝜶∥4\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})\right)\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p^{\prime}_{i}(\widehat{\mathbf{y}})\right)\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}
=2​d⋅∥Wval∥2⋅∥𝜶∥4\displaystyle=2\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}

Since 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} were arbitrary, we conclude

Δ​𝖺𝗍𝗍≤2​d⋅∥Wval∥2⋅∥𝜶∥4\Delta\mathsf{att}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{val}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}

∎

5.3.4 After the Activation Function

The activation function in the feed-forward neural network can be defined as follows. Let WgateW_{\text{gate}} and WupW_{\text{up}} be two d×dd\times d matrices. Let g⁡(𝐱)=Wgate⋅𝐱g(\mathbf{x})=W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathbf{x} for 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. For any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} the sigmoid function is defined as

𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(x)=11+e−x\mathsf{sig}(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} (9)

Note that for any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, 𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(x)∈(0,1)\mathsf{sig}(x)\in(0,1). We extend this to a vector 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} by defining 𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(𝐱)\mathsf{sig}(\mathbf{x}) to be the dd-dimensional vector whose iith element is 𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(xi)\mathsf{sig}(x_{i}). With this the activation function on 𝐱\mathbf{x} is defined as

𝖺𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐱)=Wup⋅𝐱⊙Wgate⋅𝐱⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))\mathsf{act}(\mathbf{x})=W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathbf{x}\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathbf{x}\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))

The term Wgate⋅𝐱⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathbf{x}\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x})) is known as the sigmoid linear unit or SiLU. Just like the attention mechanism, this function is applied on the normalized version of 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Therefore, we can write the activation function as

𝖺𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐱)=Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))\mathsf{act}(\mathbf{x})=W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x})) (10)

where we have re-defined g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x)} as Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x}). With this, we have the following result for Δ​𝖺𝖼𝗍\Delta\mathsf{act}.

Theorem 3.

Let 𝖺𝖼𝗍\mathsf{act} be as defined in Eq. (10). Then its global sensitivity Δ​𝖺𝖼𝗍\Delta\mathsf{act} satisfies

Δ​𝖺𝖼𝗍≤2​d⋅(d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∥𝜷∥2)2⋅∥Wup∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2\Delta\mathsf{act}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\left(\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}\right)^{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}
Proof.

For any 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have

∥𝖺𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐱)−𝖺𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐲)∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\mathsf{act}(\mathbf{x})-\mathsf{act}(\mathbf{y})}\rVert_{2} =‖Wup⋅𝖫𝖭(𝐱)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭(𝐱)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀(g(𝐱))\displaystyle=\left\lVert W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))\right.
−Wup⋅𝖫𝖭(𝐲)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭(𝐲)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀(g(𝐲))‖2\displaystyle\left.-W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_{2}
≤∥Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2}
+∥Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐲)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐲)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐲))∥2\displaystyle+\lVert{W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{y}))}\rVert_{2} (11)

which follows from the triangle inequality of the Euclidean norm. Consider the first of the two norms above

∥Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2\displaystyle\quad\lVert{W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2}
≤∥(Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱))⊙2∥2⋅∥(Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱))⊙2∥2⋅∥(𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱)))⊙2∥2\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\lVert{(W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x}))^{\odot 2}}\rVert_{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\lVert{(W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x}))^{\odot 2}}\rVert_{2}}\cdot\sqrt{\lVert{(\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x})))^{\odot 2}}\rVert_{2}}
≤∥Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥2⋅∥Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥2⋅∥𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2}
≤∥Wup∥2⋅∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2⋅∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥2⋅∥𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2}
=∥Wup∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2⋅∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥22⋅∥𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2\displaystyle=\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2}^{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2} (12)

The first inequality follows from Proposition 7, the second from Proposition 6, and the third from Eq. (3). Now from Eq. (5),

∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2} =∥𝜶⊙𝐱^+𝜷∥2\displaystyle=\lVert{\bm{\alpha}\odot\widehat{\mathbf{x}}+\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}
≤∥𝜶⊙𝐱^∥2+∥𝜷∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{\bm{\alpha}\odot\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}\rVert_{2}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}
≤d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∥𝜷∥2\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}

where the last inequality follows from Proposition 8. Thus,

∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥22≤(d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∥𝜷∥2)2\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left(\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}\right)^{2} (13)

For the other term, we have

∥𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥22\displaystyle\lVert{\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2}^{2} =∑i=1d(𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡((g⁡(𝐱))i))2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}(\mathsf{sig}((g(\mathbf{x}))_{i}))^{2}
≤∑i=1d12\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{d}1^{2} (14)
=d\displaystyle=d

Therefore ∥𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2≤d\lVert{\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}. Thus, Eq. (12) becomes

∥Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2\displaystyle\lVert{W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2} ≤∥Wup∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2⋅∥𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐱)∥22⋅∥𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐱))∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{x})}\rVert_{2}^{2}\cdot\lVert{\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{x}))}\rVert_{2}
≤d⋅(d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∥𝜷∥2)2⋅∥Wup∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{d}\cdot\left(\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}\right)^{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}

Exactly the same way, we have

∥Wup⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐲)⊙Wgate⋅𝖫𝖭⁡(𝐲)⊙𝗌𝗂𝗀⁡(g⁡(𝐲))∥2≤d⋅(d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∥𝜷∥2)2⋅∥Wup∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2\lVert{W_{\text{up}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})\odot W_{\text{gate}}\cdot\mathsf{LN}(\mathbf{y})\odot\mathsf{sig}(g(\mathbf{y}))}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\cdot\left(\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}\right)^{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}

Therefore, Eq. (11) becomes

∥𝖺𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐱)−𝖺𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐲)∥2≤2​d⋅(d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∥𝜷∥2)2⋅∥Wup∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\mathsf{act}(\mathbf{x})-\mathsf{act}(\mathbf{y})}\rVert_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\left(\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}\right)^{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}

Since 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} were arbitrary, we conclude

Δ​𝖺𝖼𝗍≤2​d⋅(d⋅∥𝜶∥4+∥𝜷∥2)2⋅∥Wup∥2⋅∥Wgate∥2\Delta\mathsf{act}\leq 2\sqrt{d}\cdot\left(\sqrt{d}\cdot\lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert_{4}+\lVert{\bm{\beta}}\rVert_{2}\right)^{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{up}}}\rVert_{2}\cdot\lVert{W_{\text{gate}}}\rVert_{2}

∎

5.4 Making the Process Differentially Private

Given the ℓ2\ell_{2}-sensitivity Δ​f\Delta f of the output 𝐱\mathbf{x} of the component ff, which serves as the input to the component being offloaded to the GPU, we first sample noise 𝜼∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,(Δ​f/ϵ)2​Id)\bm{\eta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},({\Delta f}/{\epsilon})^{2}I_{d}), where IdI_{d} is the d×dd\times d identity matrix. We then offload the vector 𝐱+𝜼\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta} to the GPU. For a prompt of nn tokens, with a single offloaded operation, this mechanism satisfies n​ϵ\sqrt{n}\epsilon-Gaussian differential privacy according to Propositions 2 and 3. The steps taken by the GPU maintain this guarantee due to the post-processing property of GDP. However, note that a given prompt is offloaded multiple times: once for each offloaded component, once for each transformer layer, and then once for each generated token. Thus, to be precise, the overall privacy guarantee should include all offloaded instances. However, we stick to the privacy guarantee of n​ϵ\sqrt{n}\epsilon-GDP and even ϵ\epsilon-GDP (i.e., keeping the privacy parameter constant, instead of scaling it with the prompt size), as otherwise an overwhelming amount of noise needs to be added, and moreover, our prompt reconstruction attacks (Section 7.4) show negligible success rate with this privacy level.

5.5 Floating Point Issues

The noise addition and cancellation procedure in our scheme as shown in Eq. (1) works perfectly for real numbers. However, in floating-point arithmetic, this may result in a phenomenon known as catastrophic cancellation (see for example [28, §4.2]). Given the quantities W​𝐱W\mathbf{x} and W⁡(𝐱+𝜼)−W​𝜼W(\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta})-W\bm{\eta} we are interested in knowing the difference between the two, when the arithmetic is done over floating point numbers. The iith element of W​𝐱W\mathbf{x} is given as ⟨𝐰i,𝐱⟩\langle{\mathbf{w}_{i}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle, where 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} is the iith row of WW. We thus consider a generic element of W​𝐱W\mathbf{x}, denoted ⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle, as the dot product of the appropriate row of WW. The corresponding value through offloading is ⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩−⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle.

To make this precise, we will use the notation 𝖿𝗅\mathsf{fl}{} to denote the variant of any function that uses two floating point numbers and outputs a floating point number as an answer. For example if xx and yy are floating point numbers, then 𝖿𝗅⁡(x+y)\mathsf{fl}(x+y) denotes the operation that adds two floating point numbers and rounds them to the nearest floating point number. Under this notation, we are interested in the quantity

|𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩)−𝖿𝗅⁡(𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩)−𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩))|\left|\mathsf{fl}({\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle})-\mathsf{fl}(\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle)-\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle))\right| (15)

Note that the outer subtraction is not over floating point numbers.

5.5.1 Background On Floating Point Arithmetic

We give a brief background on floating point arithmetic summarized from [28]. We use the binary32 number format as the foundation. A number xx in this format is written as

x=M⋅2e−p+1,x=M\cdot 2^{e-p+1},

where p=24p=24 is the precision, ee is an integer satisfying emin≤e≤emaxe_{\min}\leq e\leq e_{\max} and MM is an integer satisfying 2p−1≤|M|<2p2^{p-1}\leq|M|<2^{p}. To be precise this is called the normalized representation. For binary32 numbers we have emin=−126e_{\min}=-126 and emax=127e_{\max}=127. The unit round-off of radix-2 precision-pp floating point system in the round-to-nearest mode is defined as

u=12​21−p=2−pu=\frac{1}{2}2^{1-p}=2^{-p} (16)

This gives rise to the following standard model of floating-point arithmetic. For all floating-point numbers aa, bb such that a∗ba*b does not underflow nor overflow, we have

𝖿𝗅⁡(a∗b)=(a∗b)​(1+δ),|δ|<u\mathsf{fl}{(a*b)}=(a*b)(1+\delta),\;|\delta|<u (17)

where ∗* is one of the elementary arithmetic operations: +,−,×,÷+,-,\times,\div. Roughly, an underflow (respectively, overflow) occurs when the result is smaller (respectively, larger) than the smallest (respectively, largest) possible floating point number in the given number format.

The following definition is from [18, §3.1] (see also [28, §5.1])

Definition 6.

Let δi\delta_{i} satisfy |δi|≤u|\delta_{i}|\leq u for 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d, and assume that

d​u<1.du<1.

Then

∏i=1d(1+δi)±1=1+θd,\prod_{i=1}^{d}(1+\delta_{i})^{\pm 1}=1+\theta_{d},

where

|θd|≤d​u1−d​u=:γd.|\theta_{d}|\leq\frac{du}{1-du}=:\gamma_{d}.

∎

We will make use of the following result from [18, §3.1]:

|⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩−𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩)|≤γd​⟨|𝐰|,|𝐱|⟩\left|\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle-\mathsf{fl}({\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle})\right|\leq\gamma_{d}\langle{|\mathbf{w}|},{|\mathbf{x}|}\rangle (18)

5.5.2 Floating-Point Error Bound

Our main result is as follows

Theorem 4.

If no underflow or overflow occurs then

|𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩)−𝖿𝗅⁡(𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩)−𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩))|≤γd​⟨|𝐰|,|𝐱​|+|𝐱+𝜼|+|​𝜼|⟩+u⁡⟨|𝐰|,|𝐱|⟩+O⁡(d​u2)\displaystyle\left|\mathsf{fl}({\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle})-\mathsf{fl}(\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle)-\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle))\right|\leq\gamma_{d}\langle{|\mathbf{w}|},{|\mathbf{x}|+|\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}|+|\bm{\eta}|}\rangle+u\langle{|\mathbf{w}|},{|\mathbf{x}|}\rangle+O(du^{2})
Proof.

Let us define,

A=𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩),B=𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩),C=𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩)A=\mathsf{fl}({\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle}),B=\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle),C=\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle)

With this notation, we seek to find the bound on

|A−𝖿𝗅⁡(B−C)|\left|A-\mathsf{fl}(B-C)\right|

From one application of the standard model (Eq. (17)) we have

|A−𝖿𝗅⁡(B−C)|\displaystyle\left|A-\mathsf{fl}(B-C)\right| ≤|A−(B−C)​(1+δ)|\displaystyle\leq\left|A-(B-C)(1+\delta)\right|
=|A−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩+⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩−(B−C)​(1+δ)|\displaystyle=\left|A-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle+\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle-(B-C)(1+\delta)\right|
≤|A−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩|+|(B−C)​(1+δ)−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩|\displaystyle\leq\left|A-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\right|+\left|(B-C)(1+\delta)-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\right| (19)

where the last step follows from the triangle inequality. From Eq. (18), we have

|A−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩|=|𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩)−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩|≤γd​⟨|𝐰|,|𝐱|⟩\left|A-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\right|=\left|\mathsf{fl}({\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle})-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\right|\leq\gamma_{d}\langle{|\mathbf{w}|},{|\mathbf{x}|}\rangle (20)

We expand the second term in Eq. (19) as follows

|(B−C)​(1+δ)−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩|\displaystyle\left|(B-C)(1+\delta)-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\right| =|B−C+δ⁡(B−C)−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩|\displaystyle=\left|B-C+\delta(B-C)-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\right|
≤|B−C−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩|+|δ⁡(B−C)|\displaystyle\leq\left|B-C-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\right|+\left|\delta(B-C)\right|
=|B−C−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩+⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩−⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩|+|δ⁡(B−C)|\displaystyle=\left|B-C-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle+\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|+\left|\delta(B-C)\right|
≤|B−⟨𝐰,𝐱⟩−⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩|+|C−⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩|+|δ⁡(B−C)|\displaystyle\leq\left|B-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}}\rangle-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|+\left|C-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|+\left|\delta(B-C)\right|
=|B−⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩|+|C−⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩|+|δ⁡(B−C)|\displaystyle=\left|B-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|+\left|C-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|+\left|\delta(B-C)\right| (21)

with multiple applications of the triangle inequality. From Eq. 17, we have

|B−⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩|=|𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩)−⟨𝐰,𝐱+𝜼⟩|≤γd​⟨|𝐰|,|𝐱+𝜼|⟩\left|B-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|=\left|\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle)-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|\leq\gamma_{d}\langle{|\mathbf{w}|},{|\mathbf{x}+\bm{\eta}|}\rangle (22)

and

|C−⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩|=|𝖿𝗅⁡(⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩)−⟨𝐰,𝜼⟩|≤γd​⟨|𝐰|,|𝜼|⟩\left|C-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|=\left|\mathsf{fl}(\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle)-\langle{\mathbf{w}},{\bm{\eta}}\rangle\right|\leq\gamma_{d}\langle{|\mathbf{w}|},{|\bm{\eta}|}\rangle (23)

The remaining term in Eq. (21) can be expanded as follows, noting that |δ|≤u|\delta|\leq u from Definition 6,
